teaser: Turned down by the jury, it became the star of the first one-man show an artist ever paid for.
review_notes:
Dimensions 361 x 598 cm.
1855 Exposition Universelle: the jury accepted eleven Courbet works and refused the Studio and the Burial at Ornans; check the count of eleven.
Pavilion of Realism: about forty paintings, entry 1 franc (later reduced), poor attendance.
Delacroix's journal entry (August 1855): he stayed alone nearly an hour and called the refused picture one of the most singular works of the time; paraphrased, not quoted.
Nude painted with the help of a photograph Courbet asked his patron Bruyas to send: standard account.
Identifications on the right (Baudelaire reading, Champfleury seated, the group with Bruyas and Proudhon, the collector couple, the lovers) follow Courbet's letter to Champfleury.
The seated hunter with dogs as a disguised Napoleon III: Helene Toussaint's 1977 hypothesis, presented as a theory.
Jeanne Duval painted out at Baudelaire's request and now showing through: not pointed at, since it is not legible in this image.
Use as a backdrop in a private theater before the Louvre bought it in 1920 with the help of a public subscription: please verify.
'Newspapers are the cemeteries of ideas' is attributed to Proudhon.
Unfinished background covered with a thin reddish tone: check wording.
Skull-on-newspaper find is at about x 0.32, y 0.705 and is small.

lesson.text: In the spring of 1855, Gustave Courbet received the news he had half expected. Paris was preparing a World's Fair, with a giant art exhibition meant to show off French painting to the planet. The jury took eleven of his pictures. It refused the two biggest, the ones he cared about most. This was one of them.

He had painted it in a rush that winter, in a few months, on a canvas 3.61 meters high and almost 6 meters wide (about 12 by 20 feet). Thirty or so figures, life-size. Being told there was no room for it was, for a man with Courbet's pride, a declaration of war.

His answer had no real precedent. He rented a plot of land a short walk from the official exhibition, had a temporary building put up at his own expense, and hung about forty of his paintings inside. Over the door he wrote one word: Realism. Entry cost one franc.

Hardly anyone came, and Courbet lost money. But one visitor mattered. Eugène Delacroix, the great painter of the older generation, stayed alone in the pavilion for nearly an hour and wrote in his diary that the refused picture was one of the most remarkable works of its time.

So what had the jury turned away? Courbet gave it a strange full title: “A real allegory summing up seven years of my artistic and moral life.” An allegory is a picture where figures stand for ideas. A real allegory sounds like a contradiction, and he meant it to. The room is split into three parts, and each has a meaning.
The canvas reads like a stage with three groups of actors.

lines.label: The left
lines.text: Courbet called this side the world of everyday life: the poor and the rich, the exploited and those who exploit them. Most of them look down. None of them looks at the painting.

lines.label: The center
lines.text: The painter at work, in full light, with a model, a child and a cat around him. Everything in the room turns around this small bright island.

lines.label: The right
lines.text: His friends and supporters: writers, a philosopher, collectors, lovers. Courbet joked that these were his shareholders, the people who kept him going.

lesson.text: Notice who gets the best seat. In older pictures of crowds, the middle belonged to a king or a saint. Here it belongs to a man with a brush, and he has painted himself in profile, beard tilted up, as if the thirty people behind him were not there.
The Studio claims something new for 1855: that an artist, working from his own life and his own time, stands at the center of society and answers to no one.

The left side has a harder edge than it first appears. Among the hunters, peddlers and beggars, Courbet tucked in a small still life with a message about the press of his day, which had not been kind to him. Search the shadows just left of the big canvas.
A skull is resting on a newspaper somewhere in the left half. Where?

spots.title: Skull on a newspaper
spots.text: A pale skull sits on a crumpled paper. A friend of Courbet's had called newspapers the cemeteries of ideas, and the painter turned the joke into an object.

lesson.text: Death on one side, then. On the other side of that same easel, life is going on at full strength. The middle of the picture is where Courbet shows what he thinks painting is for, and he does it with four figures, one of them on canvas.

lesson.title: Around the easel
lesson.text: Four stops in the bright center of the room.

spots.title: The landscape
spots.text: He is not painting the model or the crowd. He is painting a valley near his hometown, Ornans, from memory, indoors. Its sky is the brightest patch of the whole canvas.

spots.title: The model
spots.text: She has dropped her clothes in a pink heap and holds a white sheet. She watches the brush instead of posing: often read as Truth, or as a muse who simply looks over his shoulder.

spots.title: The boy
spots.text: A child in worn clothes and wooden shoes stares up at the canvas. He stands for the innocent eye, the viewer who has not yet learned what art is supposed to look like.

spots.title: The cat
spots.text: A white cat plays on the floor, back turned to all this seriousness. Courbet liked to let an animal wander into his grandest scenes.

lesson.text: A nude woman, a peasant boy, a landscape: nature, truth and innocence gather around the easel while the rest of the room sits in half darkness. It is a self-portrait as boast. Courbet was known for his vanity, and for once it produced something generous too, a place of honor for his friends.

The model never stood in that room. Courbet was working far from Paris and short of time, so he asked a patron to send him a photograph of a nude. Photography was less than twenty years old, and painters were already quietly using it.

The upper half of the canvas is nearly empty: a brownish wall with ghostly shapes. Courbet ran out of time before the deadline and brushed a thin reddish tone over what he had begun there. The emptiness was an accident, and it gives the room its odd, dreamlike air.

The crowd is the long game of this picture. People have spent more than a century and a half putting names on these faces. Some names come from Courbet's own letters. Others are guesses, and one of them is explosive.

spots.title: Baudelaire
spots.text: The poet Charles Baudelaire sits on a table at the far edge, lost in a book. He is the only person here too absorbed to notice anything, which is its own kind of portrait.

spots.title: Champfleury
spots.text: Seated on a stool, hands on his knees: the writer Champfleury, the critic who defended Realism in print. Courbet described the whole painting to him in a long letter.

spots.title: The collectors
spots.text: A fashionable couple visits the studio. Her flowered shawl is the richest piece of painting on this side. They stand for the art lovers who buy.

spots.title: The lovers
spots.text: By the window, a couple embraces and ignores everyone. Courbet listed free love among the things his friends stood for.

spots.title: The hunter
spots.text: A seated man in tall boots with two dogs. In 1977 a scholar proposed that he is Emperor Napoleon III in disguise, smuggled into a picture meant for the Emperor's own fair.

spots.title: The mannequin
spots.text: Behind the easel hangs a pale figure, arms raised like a martyr. It is a studio dummy, the tool of old-fashioned academic painting, pushed out of the light.

spots.title: Hat, guitar, dagger
spots.text: A plumed hat, a guitar and a dagger lie in the dust: the props of Romantic painting, with its troubadours and duels. Courbet has thrown them on the floor.

lesson.text: Baudelaire was not painted alone. His companion, Jeanne Duval, originally stood beside him. He asked Courbet to remove her, and the painter obliged. With time the paint on top has thinned, and her faint outline has begun to show through again.

After Courbet's death the huge canvas drifted between owners, and is said to have served for a while as a backdrop in a private theater. The Louvre finally bought it in 1920, partly with money given by the public. Sixty-five years after an official jury refused it, citizens paid to bring it in.

And the pavilion with one word over its door? It lost money in 1855, but the idea outlived the debt. Twelve years later Édouard Manet built his own pavilion beside another World's Fair. An artist who shows alone, on his own terms, without waiting for a jury: that habit starts here.

quiz.question: What did Courbet do when the jury refused this painting?
options: He built his own pavilion and showed it there
He sent it to London instead
quiz.explanation: He paid for a temporary building near the World's Fair and hung about forty works under the word Realism.

quiz.question: What is Courbet painting on the easel?
options: A landscape of his home region
A portrait of the nude model
quiz.explanation: He paints a valley near Ornans from memory, ignoring the model and the crowd.

quiz.question: Who is gathered on the right side of the studio?
quiz.explanation: Writers, collectors and friends stand on the right, the people he called his shareholders.

quiz.question: What rests on a newspaper in the left half?
quiz.explanation: The skull on a newspaper turns the phrase about newspapers being cemeteries of ideas into an object.

quiz.question: How did Courbet paint the nude model?
options: With the help of a photograph
quiz.explanation: Working far from Paris, he asked a patron to send him a photograph of a nude.

quiz.question: Which older painter spent nearly an hour alone with the picture and admired it?
quiz.explanation: Delacroix praised the refused work in his diary.

facts.text: Courbet's private pavilion was a huge commercial success.
facts.explanation: Few visitors came and he lost money, though the idea of the solo show lasted.

facts.text: The empty upper wall of the painting is partly the result of Courbet running out of time.
facts.explanation: He brushed a thin tone over the unfinished background before the deadline.

facts.text: The poet Baudelaire is shown chatting with the nude model.
facts.explanation: He sits at the far right edge, absorbed in a book.
